teaching.causalExplanation: Hit often. In a solid, only the particles on the surface can be hit by the acid. The ones inside have to wait until the layers above them have reacted. So the key quantity is surface area, the total area of the solid that's exposed. Picture a one centimetre cube. It has six faces, six square centimetres of surface. Cut it into one millimetre cubes, and you get a thousand of them, with sixty square centimetres of surface altogether. Same mass, ten times the surface for the acid to hit. Here's the evidence, on the same logging balance, with the same one mole per litre acid at twenty degrees. The chips curve is the control run from last time. The powder froths hard, so the plug really matters, and its curve shoots up and flattens in about forty seconds. The chips take about six and a half minutes. But both level off at zero point four four grams, because it's the same mass of calcium carbonate, just more of it exposed at once. So more surface means more acid particles hit the solid each second. That's collision frequency again. The temperature is the same, so the fraction of collisions with enough energy hasn't changed, and neither has the activation energy. More collisions each second, at the same success rate, means a faster reaction. And surface area only matters when the reaction happens at a surface, like a solid reacting with a liquid or a gas.

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How do surface area and catalysts change reaction rate differently?" The answer, in order: crushing exposes more particles to be hit, so more collisions per second at the same Eₐ (1 to 4); a catalyst is not used up and gives a route with a lower Eₐ, so a larger fraction of the same collisions succeed (5 to 8); neither changes how much product forms (3, 9); the two combine in solid catalysts (10).

scenes.teachingReason: So more surface means more acid particles hit the solid each second. That's collision frequency again.
